title.en: Jo-wiis and the Origin of the Bird Dance

region.en: Sky council house of the birds, and the Seneca council house at New Year
region.zh: 天空的群鳥議屋與新年時的塞內卡議屋

texts.period: Converse (1908); Jo-wiis is regarded as the founder of the Eagle Society

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'Ga-do-jih and Sa-go-da-oh, the Golden Eagle and the Hunter'

summary.en: The Ga-do-jih, the Golden Eagle of the far away heavens, is the Head Chief of all the birds; to his subchief Don-yon-do, the Bald Eagle, he has assigned the mountain tops of the earth land. Among the birds of prey is Sa-go-da-oh, the Hunting Vulture, whose obnoxious duty is to plunder in offensive places - but the law of Ga-do-jih is that the earth must be kept clean. One day in the long time ago, Jo-wiis, a young Indian lad, was lost in the woods, and had wept until nearly blinded; hungering and faint he had fallen on the river bank to die, when Don-yon-do discovered him, lifting him on his wings; when no one came for the fast dying boy, Sa-go-da-oh, whose talons were long and strong but whose heart was tender, bore him to Ga-do-jih in the sky, who nourished him and grew to love him. Ga-do-jih took Jo-wiis to the sky council house when the birds were celebrating the New Year, and taught him their dances, the bird songs and all the laws of the birds, especially the sacred law protecting their nests in the spring and sheltering them in the winter; also the corn and the grains, which must be shared with the feathered folk below. Returned under the great vulture's wing while the Seven Star Brothers danced the New Year dance over the council house, Jo-wiis related his experiences to his astonished listeners, and it was decided that he should teach the people the bird dances he had learned in the sky: by this legend the Iroquois know the origin of the Bird dance, the most prominent dance of the Iroquois.
summary.zh: 遠天的金鵰加多吉是百鳥的大首領；副首領白頭鵰當永東多受命鎮守群山之巔。猛禽中還有獵鷲薩戈達奧，乾著最不體面的活——在穢處拾荒；但加多吉的律法是：大地必須潔淨。遠古的一天，少年喬威斯在林中迷途，哭得目將盲，飢渴交加倒在河岸待死。白頭鵰把他托上翅膀；無人來救時，爪利心軟的獵鷲把他抱上天空交給加多吉，鵰王哺育他、寵愛他。群鳥議新年時，鵰王攜他入天上的議屋，教他鳥舞、鳥歌與百鳥律法——尤其是春護鳥巢、冬庇群鳥的聖律，還有必須與下方羽族分享的玉米與五穀。昂宿七兄弟正在議屋上空跳新年舞時，獵鷲馱他回到雪被下的大地；族人驚訝地聽他講述天上的經歷，決議由他把鳥舞教給眾人——易洛魁最盛大的鳥舞，由此傳世。

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. The Bird dance (ga-ne-gwa-e) is the public exhibition of the Eagle Society; the sign of membership is a round spot of red paint on either cheek.

passages.text: The Ga-do-jih, the Golden Eagle of the far away heavens, is the Head Chief of all the birds. The Ga-do-jih never visits the earth, but employs many assistants upon whom he imposes various duties. To his subchief, Don-yon-do, the Bald Eagle, he has assigned the mountain tops of the earth land... From his retinue of servitors, Ga-do-jih has chosen many of the vulture family, whose obnoxious duties lead them to plunder in offensive places. But they are faithful in his service, for it is the law of Ga-do-jih that the earth must be kept clean. Yet these proud ravenous birds have tender hearts, and although their scavenger life leads them into base paths, Ga-do-jih does not deny them the pure air of the sky nor the clear waters of the earth.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 69-70; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: One day in the long time ago, Jo-wiis, a young Indian lad, was lost in the woods, and had wept until nearly blinded. For many days and nights the rain had flooded the forest, and Jo-wiis could not find his home path. In the black sky there was no sun or moon to guide him, and hungering and faint, he had fallen on the river bank to die, when Don-yon-do, who chanced to be flying across the earth, discovered him, and lifting him on his wings, flew in search of an Indian village... The rain continued to fall, and no one had come for the fast dying boy when Sa-go-da-oh, winging past in search of night prey, espied him and closing in his wings, dropped to the wet earth where the boy was lying. Though Sa-go-da-oh's talons were long and strong, his heart was tender, and gently lifting Jo-wiis, bore him to the village, but failing to find his home, took him to Ga-do-jih in the sky, who nourished him and grew to love him.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 70; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Ga-do-jih took Jo-wiis to the sky council house when the birds were celebrating the New Year, and taught him their dances; also to all the feasts throughout the year, teaching him the bird songs and all the laws of the birds, especially the sacred law protecting their nests in the spring and sheltering them in the winter. And he was shown the corn and the grains, which Ga-do-jih told him must be shared with the feathered folk below. All these laws he was enjoined to impart to his people when he should return to the earth... Earth was sleeping beneath her snow blanket when Jo-wiis returned. Her streams were frozen, and her forests silent save for the keen voice of the wind which wandered through their leafless loneliness. Seeing a light in the well remembered council house where the people were holding a feast Jo-wiis entered and related to his astonished listeners his experiences in the sky... it was decided that he should teach the people the bird dances he had learned in the sky, as also the songs the sky birds sing in their councils.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 70-71; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: By this legend, the Iroquois know the origin of Je-gi-yah-goh-o-a-noh, the Bird dance, which was brought by Jo-wiis from the land of the sky birds, and is the most prominent dance of the Iroquois. It is celebrated at their New Year feast, and during its performance the dancers imitate the motions of a bird, squatting low and moving their bodies and heads as if picking the grains of corn which have been scattered on the floor. This dance reminds the people of the law of Ga-do-jih, that the Indian must nourish and care for the birds in the winter as well as in the summer time.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 72; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Ga-nus-quah and the Go-gon-sa: The Stone Giant and the First False Faces
title.zh: 石巨人加努斯誇與第一副假臼

region.en: Cave in the Alleghany mountains, and the basswood forests
region.zh: 阿利根尼山中的石穴與椴樹林

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'Ga-nus-quah and Go-gon-sa, the Stone Giants and False Faces'

summary.en: Tall, fierce and hostile, they were a powerful tribe, the Stone Giants! Cannibals who would devour men, women and children, they threatened the annihilation of the Confederacy. The Shawnees have a legend of them: once gentle and hospitable, they migrated to the far northwest snow fields where the extreme cold 'froze away their humanity,' and they became 'men of icy hearts'; rolling in the sand to harden their flesh, their bodies became covered with scales which resisted the arrows of an enemy. When Tarenyawagon, Upholder of the Heavens, beheld the Iroquois' distress, he transformed himself to a stone giant, came down to the earth and united with their tribe; made their chief, he brandished his club high in the air - 'Now we will destroy the Iroquois, make a great feast of them' - and led them to hide in a deep hollow near a fort of the Onondagas; before day he scaled a high place above them and overwhelmed them with a great mass of rocks. Only one escaped, who fled to the Alleghany mountains, where he remained and grew in huge strength: Ga-nus-quah, the Depredator, vulnerable only on the bottom of his foot; to look upon his face would be instant death. It was the fate of a young hunter, a chief, blinded and bruised by hail, to seek shelter in the hollow of a great rock during a terrific storm - the cave of Ga-nus-quah. 'No human being has ever looked upon me. I kill with one glance... You came here for shelter; I will not turn you away. I will spare your life, which now is mine, but henceforth you must obey my commands... Whichever of these you meet on your way, do not pass until you have felled a strong tree and carved its image in the wood grain... Go, now, and teach the mankind people kindness, the brother goodness of all dumb things, and so win your way to live forever!' When the young hunter opened his eyes he was standing beside a basswood tree which gradually transformed to a great mask: it could see behind the stars, create storms and summon sunshine, knew the remedy for each disease, and could overpower Death - 'My tree, the basswood, is soft, and will transform for the molder... My tree wood is the life of the Go-gon-sa. Of all in the forest there is none other.' Many years he wandered carving go-gon-sa-so-oh, the false faces, from the basswood, learning the voices of all the forest trees; he who entered the cave a youth had become a bent old man, a giant in stature, when he reached his home and related his story - and became the founder of the False Face Company.
summary.zh: 身量高大、兇暴敵對——石巨人是一支強大的部族！食人的怪物吞噬男女老幼，幾乎滅絕五族同盟。肖尼人的傳說：他們昔日溫和好客，北遷雪原後嚴寒「凍去了人性」，成了「冰心之人」；滾沙硬身，體生鱗甲，箭矢難傷。當「擎天者」塔雷尼亞瓦岡見族人危殆，化身石巨人混入其族；被推為酋長後，他高舉木棒——「現在我們去誅滅易洛魁人，設人肉大宴」——領他們藏於奧農達加堡旁的深谷，黎明前登上高處，以巨岩崩落將其盡滅。僅一人逃入阿利根尼山的洞穴，長成巨力，是為掠奪者加努斯誇——只有腳底可傷，見其面者立死。一位少年酋長在冰雹中瞎眼受傷，誤入其岩穴。巨聲警告：「無人見過我的臉；我一眼殺人……你是來避難的，我不趕你走。我饒你一命，但從今你須聽命於我……路遇何物，須先伐一株強樹、在木紋中刻下它的形象……去教人類以仁慈，教他們待萬物如手足，如此方能永生！」少年睜眼時立在一株椴樹旁——樹漸化作一面巨假臼：能透視星後、興雲召日、知百病之方、能勝死亡。「我的樹是椴，質軟易化，木心多孔，日光可入……椴木就是假臼的生命，林中無出其右。」他成年累月地雕刻假臼、辨識群樹之音；入洞的少年歸鄉時已成偉岸老者——假臼社由此而立。

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. Parker notes the proper word for medicine masks is the basswood, and that the mask must first be carved on the living tree with invocation and tobacco.

passages.text: Tall, fierce and hostile, they were a powerful tribe, the Stone Giants! They invaded the country of the Iroquois during the early days of the Confederation of the Five Nations, the Mohawks, Onondagas, Oneidas, Cayugas, and Senecas, who had sent their warriors against them only to be defeated, and they threatened the annihilation of the Confederacy. They were feared, not because of their prodigious size, but they were cannibals as well, and would devour men, women and children. The Shawnees have a legend of these Giants which describes them as at one time living in a peaceful state, and although powerful, were gentle, and hospitable in their intercourse with the neighboring tribes; but from some disturbing cause they became restless, abandoned their home, and migrated to the far northwest snow fields, where the extreme cold of the winters 'froze away their humanity,' and they became 'men of icy hearts.'... In the summer they would roll in the sand to harden their flesh, and their bodies became covered with scales which resisted the arrows of an enemy.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 74-75; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: The Iroquois were being rapidly depleted in their numbers when Tarenyawagon, Upholder of the Heavens, who had bestowed upon them their hunting grounds and fisheries, beholding their distress, determined to relieve them of the merciless invaders, and transforming himself to a stone giant, came down to the earth and united with their tribe. Wonderstruck at his marvelous display of power, they made him their chief; and he brandished his club high in the air, saying, 'Now we will destroy the Iroquois, make a great feast of them, and invite all the Stone Giants of the sky.' In pretense of this intention, the Sky Holder led them to a strong fort of the Onondagas where he bade them hide in a deep hollow in the valley and await the sunrise... But before day, he scaled a high place above them and overwhelmed them with a great mass of rocks. Only one escaped, who fled to the Alleghany mountains. There he secreted himself in a cave, where he remained and grew in huge strength, when he was transformed to the myth Giant, Ga-nus-quah.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 75-76; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: During a terrific storm, the young hunter, a chief, blinded and bruised by the hail which fell like sharp flints, and having lost the trail, sought shelter within the hollow of a great rock... suddenly the rock began to move, and from a far recess a strange sound approached him... During a pause in the weird harmony, the marveling young hunter heard a voice addressing him in a stentorian strain, saying: 'Young warrior, beware! You are in the cave of the Stone Giant, Ga-nus-quah! Close your eyes. No human being has ever looked upon me. I kill with one glance. Many have wandered into this cave; no one lives to leave it. You did not come to hunt me; you came here for shelter; I will not turn you away. I will spare your life, which now is mine, but henceforth you must obey my commands... Whichever of these you meet on your way, do not pass until you have felled a strong tree and carved its image in the wood grain. When you first strike the tree, if it speaks, it will be my voice urging you and you must go on with your task. When the trees were first set in their earth mold, each was given a voice... Go, now, and teach the mankind people kindness, the brother goodness of all dumb things, and so win your way to live forever!'
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 76-77; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: When the young hunter opened his eyes, he was standing beside a basswood tree which gradually transformed to a great mask, and related to him its power. It could see behind the stars. It could create storms, and summon the sunshine. It empowered battles or weakened the forces at will. It knew the remedy for each disease, and could overpower Death. It knew all the poison roots and could repel their strong evils... The venomous reptiles knew its threat and crept from its path. It said: 'My tree, the basswood, is soft, and will transform for the molder. My tree wood is porous, and the sunlight can enter its darkness... My tree wood is the life of the Go-gon-sa. Of all in the forest there is none other.' With this knowledge, the young hunter started on his way carving go-gon-sa-so-oh (false faces). From the basswood he hewed them. By the voice of the Stone Giant he was guided to choose; and well he learned the voices of all the forest trees before he completed his task... Many years had passed in the laborious task, and he who entered the cave a youth, had become a bent old man when, burdened with the go-gon-sas he had carved, he set out on his return to his people. Year after year his burden had grown heavier, but his back broadened in strength, and he had become a giant in stature when he reached his home and related his story.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 78-79; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: De-wan-do and the Flying Head: The Acorns That Were Coals
title.zh: 德萬多與飛首：被誤當橡實的炭火

region.en: Broad river and forest of the early Long House
region.zh: 長屋初立時的大河與森林

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'Ko-nea-raw-neh, the Flying Heads'

summary.en: The Long House was new and the people were tranquil in its peace when they were terrorized by the visitations of the Flying Heads. These odious Heads were enveloped in long, fire-flaming hair which streamed to the wind in their flying, dazzling and blinding those who dared look at them; and armed with two great bearlike paws, which were ever in motion as if clutching at prey, they shot through the air like meteors. Feasts, invocations and incantations were of no avail; drums, rattles and loud screaming shouts gave forth no sound when the Heads appeared; arrows and spears would glance from their fiery hair, or break like a dead branch. One night at the sundown, De-wan-do, an Iroquois woman with her infant swung across her shoulders, was paddling her canoe across a broad river when a big face lifted from the water, whose flaming hair streaked the waves like serpents of fire. Pressing her infant close she sprang to the shore and fled, throwing it piece after piece of deer meat, her blanket, her doeskin dress, leggings, moccasins - until, despairing, she remembered the charm of an infant's moccasin to avert danger, and hastily removing one from her child's foot, threw it behind her: the Head stopped, and reeling and wandering as if blinded, fell to the ground. When it overtook her lodge, De-wan-do was roasting acorns at the hearth, drawing them away one by one and eating them as they burst their shells; the astonished Head, approaching behind her, wondered, for it thought she was eating the live coals. 'They must be good,' thought the Head, 'and I'll have my share'; and gathering the hot coals with its paws, thrust them into its mouth when, screaming in agony, it fled from the lodge in a great blaze of fire which drifted into the night. And the Head never returned: it is believed that the live coals it had mistaken for acorns burned it to death.
summary.zh: 長屋初成、萬民安泰之時，飛首降臨為禍。這些醜惡的頭顱裹著噴火的長髮，飛掠時灼人雙目；一雙巨熊般的掌爪時時開合，如攫獵物，流星般劃空而過。盛宴、祝禱、咒語都無濟於事；飛首現身時，鼓聲鈴響一齊喑啞，箭矛不是滑過火髮便是折斷如枯枝。一日黃昏，易洛魁婦人德萬多背著嬰兒划舟渡河，一張巨首自水面升起，火髮在波上如群蛇竄燃。她緊摟嬰兒躍上岸奔逃，一路拋下鹿肉、毯子、鹿皮衣、鞋襪——直到窮急之中想起嬰兒鞋能避邪，急忙脫下孩子的一隻小鞋拋在身後：飛首頓時止步，暈頭轉向跌倒在地。等它追到她的屋子，德萬多正在灶前炒橡實——一顆顆爆殼剝出就吃；跟在身後的飛首驚訝不已：它以為她在吃炭火。「這一定好吃，」它想，「我也得來一份」；便用掌爪捧起滾燙的炭塞進嘴裡——慘叫一聲，化成一團沖天的烈焰逃出屋去。飛首從此未再回來：據信它是被誤當橡實的炭火燒死了。

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. In some myths the flying heads are false faces; the Mohawks instead of making the Stone Giant the founder credit the Flying Heads with being the original False Faces.

passages.text: The Long House was new and the people were tranquil in its peace when they were terrorized by the visitations of the Flying Heads. These odious Heads were enveloped in long, fire-flaming hair which streamed to the wind in their flying, dazzling and blinding those who dared look at them; and armed with two great bearlike paws, which were ever in motion as if clutching at prey, they shot through the air like meteors. When flying, these Heads were of enormous size, yet, upon the land or among the forest trees, they could become no larger than the head of a bear... but whether in the air or upon the land, there seemed no human power able to combat them, and the people fled in horror whenever they appeared.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 79; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Feasts, invocations and incantations were of no avail; drums, rattles and loud screaming shouts gave forth no sound when the Heads appeared, and they heeded them not. Arrows and spears would glance from their fiery hair, or break like a dead branch wind-blown from the tree, and there seemed no succor for the people... One night at the sundown, De-wan-do, an Iroquois woman, with her infant wrapped in a blanket and swung across her shoulders, was paddling her canoe across a broad river. She was hastening before the darkness should set in when, as she neared the shore, a long shadow swept across her canoe and a big face lifted from the water, a face whose flaming hair streaked the waves like serpents of fire and hissed to vapors the smooth-flowing river.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 79-80; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Like all her people, De-wan-do knew the Flying Heads, and pressing her infant close to her breast, she sprang to the shore and ran to the forest... Looking back and seeing the Head following her, she threw it a piece of deer meat, which, as it stopped to devour it, delayed it for a time... through all the night she ran, still pursued by the Head... She threw it her blanket, in rage it tore it to fragments; then her doeskin dress, her leggings, moccasins, piece by piece all the clothes she wore... and the Head had nearly overtaken her when, despairing, she remembered the charm of an infant's moccasin to avert danger, and hastily removing one from her child's foot, threw it behind her. At its sight the Head stopped, and in rage beat the air with its great paws. In vain it tried to avoid the moccasin, and reeling and wandering as if blinded, fell to the ground.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 81; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: But De-wan-do heard not. Suffering with hunger from her long fasting, she was at the hearth fire roasting acorns, while her infant lay sleeping near the fire. One by one as they burst their shells she drew them away and ate them, and the astonished Head, approaching behind her, wondered, for it thought she was eating the live coals. 'They must be good,' thought the Head, 'and I'll have my share'; and gathering the hot coals with its paws, thrust them into its mouth when, screaming in agony, it fled from the lodge in a great blaze of fire which drifted into the night! And the Head never returned. It is believed that the live coals it had mistaken for acorns burned it to death.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 81; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: The Face in the Water and the Origin of the Death Dance
title.zh: 水中之臉與死亡之舞的起源

region.en: Health-giving spring in the hollow of a rock, and the fires below
region.zh: 岩穴中的治病靈泉與地下之火

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'The Face in the Water and the Death Dance'

summary.en: In the hollow of a rock in a forest was a health-giving spring known to all red men. This spring, which possessed mysterious power, was protected by two spirits: from sunrise to noon, Oh-swe-da, spirit of the spruce tree, was its guardian, and this was its 'charm time'; but after the noon, when the shadows slanted across it and Och-do-ah, the Bat, had entered the rock, the spring became a baneful poison, sudden or lingering, as Och-do-ah might will. Ah-ne-ah, Rose Flower, went to the spring to weave sweet-smelling grasses into baskets, singing the firefly song, and did not see the noon nearing: as she held her elm bowl to the gurgling water, it seemed never to fill, and she saw there a face more beautiful than any she had ever beheld, smiling and nodding at her - and the threatening shadow entered the spring, and something suddenly seized her and bore her upward far from the forest, plunged down its cataract to a wide water, and led her down below the earth to a place glaring as with flames where numberless people were dancing carelessly - among them some of her own people who had died years before, appealing to her for pity as they moaned 'don-de-gwan-de, don-de-gwan-de' (pity us, pity us). Doomed to the fire dance, she felt herself blind and dying, when she seemed to breathe a new air, life restoring and fragrant of pines of the woodland, and opening her eyes it was sunrise and she stood by the spring! Beside her was a young warrior with an owl wing and an eagle wing, the face that had smiled to her from the spring - Oh-swe-da, who had welcomed her only to warn: Och-do-ah, the Bat, poisons the spring water when the sun turns away, and had sent one of his helpers to take her to the fires below where the witches were dancing the death dance; he had snatched her from the witch fire - but the penalty for lingering too late at the spring must be paid. Soon after a pestilence came to her people, and day by day the beautiful Ah-ne-ah was fading away, until one summer morning at the vanishing of the dew Ah-ne-ah disappeared: by the side of her couch were two fallen feathers, one of the owl, the other an eagle. But the faithful Ah-ne-ah had related to her people the terrible story of the witch fire, and taught them its dance which could no more destroy them: thus originated the Oh-gi-we, the Death dance of the Iroquois, one of the rites of their Death watch which releases a departed spirit from the evil influences of the witches.
summary.zh: 林中岩穴裡有一泓紅人皆知的治病靈泉。泉有二靈守護：自日出至正午，雲杉之靈奧斯維達司泉，是為「靈驗之時」；正午過後，陰影斜罩、蝙蝠奧克多阿入岩，泉水便成了致死的毒——速死或緩死，全憑奧克多阿之意。「玫瑰花」阿內阿去泉邊編織香草籃、唱著流螢之歌，不覺日已近午：她把榆木碗伸向汩汩泉水，水卻總也盛不滿——她看見水中有一張前所未見的美麗面孔，含笑向她點頭。威脅的暗影罩入泉中，微笑隱沒；有物猛然抓住她，凌空帶她遠離森林，俯衝過瀑落入闊水，再引她下行地底——一片火光之地，無數人在那裡漫不經心地起舞，其中竟有她族中死去多年的故人，哀號著「可憐我們，可憐我們」。她被判入火舞，眼將盲、命將絕，忽然吸到一股新氣——松林般復甦的芬芳——睜眼時已日出，她立在泉邊！身旁立著一位獵人裝束的少年戰士，一翼鴞、一翼鵰——正是泉中含笑的那張臉：雲杉之靈奧斯維達，他迎接她只為示警——太陽偏轉時蝙蝠便毒化泉水，且已遣使者要把她送往下界巫火中跳死亡之舞；他把她從巫火中奪回——但遲留泉邊的代價必須償還。不久瘟疫降於其族，美麗的阿內阿日漸枯萎，一個夏晨露散之時悄然消失——榻旁只剩兩根落羽，一根鴞羽、一根鵰羽。但她已把巫火的可怕故事與那支舞教給族人——自那時起，巫火再不能害他們。易洛魁的死亡之舞「奧吉威」由此起源：那是他們「守喪」儀式中的一支，為亡者之靈解除巫者邪力的束縛。

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. The Oh-gi-we is a society with regular leaders and fixed rites, sometimes called the 'Talkers with the Dead.'

passages.text: In the hollow of a rock in a forest, was a health-giving spring known to all red men. This spring, which possessed mysterious power, was protected by two spirits. From sunrise to noon, Oh-swe-da, spirit of the spruce tree, was its guardian, and this was its 'charm time'; but after the noon, when 'the shadows slanted across it' and Och-do-ah, the Bat, had entered the rock, the spring became a baneful poison, sudden or lingering, as Och-do-ah might will. No mortal should near it for healing when Och-do-ah was coming all things to drink of its death.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 81-82; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Ah-ne-ah, Rose Flower, who had gone to the spring in quest of its water, was weaving the sweet-smelling grasses into baskets and singing the firefly song as she braided the strands to its tune, and, as happy as she was beautiful, had not seen the noon nearing the spring... As she held her elm bowl to the gurgling water, it seemed never to fill, and she saw there a face more beautiful than any she had ever beheld; and the face was smiling and nodding at her as it floated from side to side of the spring, as if coaxing... As she wondering gazed, the threatening shadow entered the spring, and when the smiling face vanished, something suddenly seized her and bore her upward far from the forest and, as with wings, so swiftly flying, the wind which seemed following lagged far behind them. Then hurrying to the earth below, they crossed a broad river and plunged down its cataract to a wide water, which raged in a fury of confusion.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 82; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: There again was the face, which led her down below the earth to a place glaring as with flames and where numberless people were dancing, carelessly dancing, and among the vast multitude passing, were some of her own people who had died years before, and who appealed to her for pity as they moaned, 'don-de-gwan-de, don-de-gwan-de' (pity us, pity us). Helpless and dumb in her terror, some monster pushed her into the circle of dancers where, doomed to the fire dance, she felt herself blind and dying, when she seemed to breathe a new air, life restoring and fragrant of pines of the woodland, and as she opened her eyes it was sunrise and she stood by the spring!
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 82-83; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: By her side was a young warrior robed as the hunter robes for the hunt... on his head were two wings, one of the owl, the other an eagle... as Ah-ne-ah looked into his eyes she beheld the face that had smiled to her from the spring! The owl and eagle-winged warrior took her hand, and as he gently led her to the edge of the forest, related to her the mystery of her strange night journey. He was Oh-swe-da, the Spirit of the Spruce, and guarded the spring from the sunrise to its noon... Och-do-ah, the Bat, was hovering in the shadow which was so near, and Och-do-ah would destroy. He poisoned the spring water when the sun turned away... But Oh-swe-da was freed from the spring, and followed to her rescue. He had snatched her from the witch fire, and now she was here! But the penalty for lingering too late at the spring must be paid - Och-do-ah would have his prey. She had escaped him, but was doomed!... Soon after, there came a pestilence to her people, and a famine was upon them. Hundreds fell victims to an epidemic, and day by day the beautiful Ah-ne-ah was fading away, until one summer morning at the vanishing of the dew Ah-ne-ah disappeared... But by the side of her couch were two fallen feathers, one of the owl, the other an eagle! But the faithful Ah-ne-ah had related to her people the terrible story of the witch fire, and taught them its dance which could no more destroy them. Thus originated the Oh-gi-we, the Death dance of the Iroquois, one of the rites of their Death watch which releases a departed spirit from the evil influences of the witches.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 83-84; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Ton-da-yent, the Twelve Warriors and the White Rabbit
title.zh: 通達揚特：十二戰士與白兔

region.en: Burial ground of the war chief, with the young pine planted above him
region.zh: 戰酋墓塚與其上的幼松

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'Ton-da-yent, the Twelve Warriors and the White Rabbit'

summary.en: In his youth he had been evil, but when grown to manhood, he had conquered his bad and becoming a warrior had won great victories for his people. Now he had passed from his people, the Ton-da-yent, the war chief! The wailers had wept, the death song had been chanted, the war paint lined his strong face, and they had crowned him with the heron feathers, the Iroquois emblem of power; in his hands they laid his stone scalping knife and war club, and robed in deerskin, his dead body waited the sunrise. When the sun neared the east sky, they wrapped the dead warrior in the bark of the elm and lowered it into the earth, and an aged priestess, Mo-non-di-ont, scattered small lumps of clay above him, to propitiate the elements, earth, air and water, through which his spirit must journey to its rest; at twilight they planted above him a young pine. A council of condolence was called at which his successor would be named, when an unknown person appeared, claiming to be the twin brother of the dead chief and demanding that he be given his name by right of twin succession - the people marveled greatly at the wonderful resemblance he bore to the dead chief, and save a glowering fire which lurked in the glance of his eye, it seemed indeed that the Ton-da-yent had returned, and the council did not hesitate to grant his request.
summary.zh: 他年少時曾經為惡，成年後卻戰勝了心魔，成為屢建戰功的戰士。如今他離開了族人——這就是戰爭大酋長通達揚特！哀哭者泣、喪歌已唱，戰紋描上他剛毅的面孔，蒼鷺羽冠——易洛魁權力的徽記——加於其頂；他手中放置石質剝皮刀與戰棒，鹿皮裹身，靜候日出。旭日將升之際，他們以榆樹皮裹屍入土；年邁的女祭司莫農迪昂特在其上撒下小塊黏土，取悅其魂必經的土、氣、水三行；暮色中又在其上植下一株幼松——通達揚特是勇士，過路人該知道他長眠於此。哀悼議會召開、將立繼任人之際，一個陌生人現身，自稱是亡酋的孿生兄弟，要求依「孿生繼承」之權承其名——族人驚異於他與亡者的酷似；除了他眼中潛藏的一團怒火，儼然就是通達揚特歸來。議會毫不遲疑地允其所請。

passages.text: In his youth he had been evil, but when grown to manhood, he had conquered his bad and becoming a warrior had won great victories for his people. An unyielding leader, he was feared by his foes. Now he had passed from his people, the Ton-da-yent, the war chief! The wailers had wept, the death song had been chanted, the war paint lined his strong face, and they had crowned him with the heron feathers, the Iroquois emblem of power. In his hands they laid his stone scalping knife and war club, and robed in deerskin, his dead body waited the sunrise. All the night long it solemnly waited.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 84; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: When the sun neared the east sky, they wrapped the dead warrior in the bark of the elm and lowered it into the earth, and an aged priestess, Mo-non-di-ont, scattered small lumps of clay above him, to propitiate the elements, earth, air and water, through which his spirit must journey to its rest. At twilight when the sun had gone, they planted above him a young pine; Ton-da-yent had been a brave warrior, and the passers must know that he was lying there.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 84-85; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: A council of condolence was called, at which his successor would be named, when an unknown person appeared, claiming to be the twin brother of the dead chief, and demanded that he be given his name by right of twin succession. The people marveled greatly at the wonderful resemblance he bore to the dead chief and, save a glowering fire which lurked in the glance of his eye, it seemed indeed that the Ton-da-yent had returned, and the council did not hesitate to grant his request.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 85; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
